To fix Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

Show details

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

Participants were presented with sets of six pseudowords and selected the items that elicited the most positive and most negative emotional responses; they subsequently provided a plausible definition for each selected item using an affirmative sentence.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 3 imprecise p values out of 13 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < .05 Nine of the ten quality associations were significant at the p < .05 level, with MiniLM-L12 as the exception, and eight of the ten specificity associations were significant, with MiniLM-L12 and MPNet as the exceptions.
p < .05 For definition quality, 120 of the 121 correlations were positive, and 102 had p < .05.
p < .05 All 110 off-diagonal quality correlations were positive, and 92 were significant with p < .05.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .804 Spearman correlations between fastText-predicted iconicity and these new measures were negligible for both definition quality (ρ = .008, p = .804) and specificity (ρ = -.005, p = .886) and were significantly smaller than those obtained using the pseudoword vectors (p < .001).
p = .886 Spearman correlations between fastText-predicted iconicity and these new measures were negligible for both definition quality (ρ = .008, p = .804) and specificity (ρ = -.005, p = .886) and were significantly smaller than those obtained using the pseudoword vectors (p < .001).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 3 code files.

File name setwd() calls found
power_analysis.R setwd(“path/to/results”)
MixedModels.R setwd(“/your/path/to/results”)
confirmatory_analyses.R setwd(“/results”)

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 3 code files.

Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. What we found

  • We classified 65 files: 20 data, 14 code, 30 documentation, 1 materials.

Share the underlying data as CSV (or a documented .sav/.dta) with a codebook so it can be reused without R: all_loo_compare.RData, all_mdl.RData, all_mdl_no_POS.RData, noweight_mdl.RData. We ran automated data-quality checks on 158 columns; 8 columns have at least one potential issue (6 columns with inconsistent category casing; 3 columns with leading/trailing whitespace; 2 columns with numeric values stored as text; 1 column whose values look like personal information). This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 158 columns across 16 data files.

Issues Identified

8 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • additional_analyses.py reads openai-gpt_results_nwords.csv.
  • plots.py reads results_models_words_Julia.csv.
  • OED_processing.R reads OED_all.csv.
  • OED_processing.Rmd reads OED_all.csv.
  • processing_raw_ratings.R reads raw_ratings_full_01_12_2022.csv.
  • rating_descriptive_stats.R reads winter_2017_iconicity.csv.
  • rating_descriptive_stats.Rmd reads winter_2017_iconicity.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A file may have been renamed.

  • calculate_ICCs.R reads iconicity_ratings_raw_deanonymized_with_NAs.csv; your deposit holds iconicity_ratings_raw.csv.
  • calculate_ICCs.Rmd reads iconicity_ratings_raw_deanonymized_with_NAs.csv; your deposit holds iconicity_ratings_raw.csv.

Check whether they are the same file. If so, use one name in both the script and the deposit.

A script starts a program outside R or Python.

  • confirmatory_analyses.R starts /snap/bin/julia.
  • power_analysis.R starts /snap/bin/julia.

Our computer does not have this program, and neither will most readers’. Name the program, its version and where to get it in the README. A Docker image can include it.

R or Python could not read a script, because of a mistake in the code itself.

  • MixedModels.R

Run each script once in a fresh session before you deposit it; the error message shows the line to fix.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • bayesian_models.R
  • bayesian_models.Rmd

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

A script downloads data while it runs.

  • confirmatory_analysis.py
  • embeddings_compare_models.py

Online files can move, change or disappear. Save the downloaded files, add them to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copies.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

  • pp_checks.R

The error message of each script is in the table above.

Other problems in the files

  • confirmatory_analyses.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.
  • MixedModels.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.
  • power_analysis.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

setwd() in the code

3 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set
power_analysis.R 1 path/to/results
MixedModels.R 1 /your/path/to/results
confirmatory_analyses.R 1 /results

Calls that install packages in the code

3 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt). 2 scripts need the internet, which is off during the run: confirmatory_analysis.py, embeddings_compare_models.py. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this.

More detail

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited (currently, a warning is provided regardless of whether the replication/reproduction study is already cited).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI. If you run the ref_doi_check module in a pipeline before this, it will use the enhanced DOI list from that module, otherwise it will only run on references with existing DOIs.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Iconicity, the perceived resemblance between a word's form and meaning, is systematically related to the semantic organization of familiar vocabulary. This raises the possibility that iconicity-related regularities also constrain how people interpret unfamiliar words. We tested this proposal by learning mappings from (sub)lexical representations to large-scale English iconicity ratings and examining whether predicted iconicity for pseudowords was associated with the semantic quality and specificity of human-generated definitions. Higher iconicity predicted from semantic representations was associated with definitions that aligned more closely with their target pseudowords and distinguished them more selectively from alternative forms. In contrast, orthographic features predicted iconicity in familiar words but showed no corresponding associations with pseudoword definitions. The positive associations for semantic representations generalized across multiple encoders, including analyses in which different models were used to predict iconicity and evaluate definitions. These findings suggest that iconicity-related semantic structure in familiar vocabulary is associated with the construction of meanings for unfamiliar forms. They are consistent with discriminative and complementary learning accounts in which previously acquired form-meaning relations provide graded constraints on novel interpretations and, more broadly, they connect theories of iconicity grounded in perceptual and experiential resemblance with distributional accounts of lexical knowledge, suggesting that linguistic experience organizes and supports the generalization of resemblance-related semantic information to novel forms.

Introduction

I recall when my wife told me how, during an official celebration in a village near Pavia, a man named Marièt approached the poorly dressed mayor and asked him in the Pavese dialect, "ghevat no un gram gabænæï da mæt sü?" (roughly, "Didn't you have a bad gabænæï to put on?"). Although the situation provided clues to its interpretation, its intended meaning was immediately clear. That is, the unfamiliar form gabænæï itself seemed particularly appropriate for what it was meant to convey. A word without an established meaning can indeed seem meaningful, (possibly) because people draw on patterns already present in familiar vocabulary, including contextual cues (e.g., Snefjella et al., 2020) and associations between forms and meanings that contribute to its perceived iconicity (e.g., Vinson et al., 2021). In the present study, we focus on the latter aspect and develop the idea that (sub)lexical patterns associated with iconicity in familiar vocabulary may help constrain the meanings people construct for unfamiliar, novel words.

Pseudo-(or novel) words (i.e., readable strings of letters that follow the orthographic and phonological regularities of a language while lacking an established lexical entry) offer a particularly informative way to investigate this process (Marson et al., 2026; Martínez-Tomás et al., 2025).

Previous studies have shown that these stimuli activate semantic information during implicit processing (Gatti et al., 2023), elicit systematic affective judgments (Gatti, Raveling, et al., 2024; Loulidi-Fernández et al., under review; van Eijkelenburg et al., 2026; see also Joosse et al., 2025, for related evidence from fictional characters' names; and Gatti et al., in press, for related evidence on spatial judgments), and support explicit choices about meaning (Bonandrini et al., 2026; Gatti, Rodio, et al., 2024). More directly, de Varda et al. (2024) demonstrated that people generate definitions whose semantic representations are more closely aligned with the intended pseudoword than with other items (see also Martínez-Tomás et al., 2026; Stagnitto et al., 2027). The question emerging from this evidence thus concerns what makes a particular form more compatible with the interpretation that a speaker constructs, and which properties of familiar vocabulary can (eventually) explain this variation.

An unfamiliar string can recruit knowledge acquired through the words that a speaker already knows.

The Complementary Learning Systems, for example, highlights that the neocortex taps into existing conceptual knowledge, using it as a structural foundation to generate new meanings (Davis & Gaskell, 2009; McClelland et al., 2020). This previously stored knowledge can be accessed through different pathways, including lexical resemblance (i.e., coactivation of lexical neighbors; Bailey & Hahn, 2001) and recurring associations between subword units and semantic features (i.e., iconicity; Sidhu, 2025). For example, English phonaesthemes such as gl-, occurring in words related to light and vision, illustrate how repeated correspondences acquire psychological relevance even outside compositional morphology (e.g., Bergen, 2004), and, more broadly, form-meaning mappings contain statistical regularities distributed across the vocabulary (Monaghan et al., 2014). Within this context, distributional semantic models provide a computational account of how linguistic experience can support such generalization by learning representations from patterns of contextual usage (Günther et al., 2019), and models incorporating subword information, such as fastText, also construct representations for unfamiliar strings from the distributional histories of their constituent character sequences (Bojanowski et al., 2017), making it possible to connect familiar lexical knowledge with the semantic information evoked by unfamiliar forms.

Within this account of form-meaning mapping, it is crucial to distinguish iconicity -the perceived resemblance between aspects of a linguistic form and its meaning -from systematicity -statistical correspondences between forms and semantic or functional properties (Dingemanse, 2012; Dingemanse et al., 2015; Emmorey, 2014; Winter et al., 2026). These properties can overlap (McLean & Motamedi, 2026), but recurring associations can guide interpretation through learned correspondences based on statistical co-occurrence of sublexical features in language use (Dingemanse et al., 2015; Winter & Perlman, 2021), whereas iconicity additionally concerns the experience that a form resembles what it conveys (Dingemanse et al., 2020; Occhino et al., 2017).

Research across spoken and signed languages has established iconicity as a pervasive dimension of linguistic organization (de Varda & Marelli, 2025; Perniss et al., 2010; Perniss & Vigliocco, 2014), with graded variation across familiar vocabulary (Perry et al., 2015). Its cognitive relevance includes proposed contributions to identifying referents and establishing new lexical representations (Imai & Kita, 2014), supported by several possible perceptual, associative, and linguistic mechanisms (Sidhu & Pexman, 2018a).

Crucially, iconicity is patterned by semantics: words referring to sensory experiences, particularly sound and touch, tend to receive higher iconicity ratings (Hinojosa et al., 2021; Winter et al., 2017), while semantic neighborhood structure also relates to perceived iconicity (Sidhu & Pexman, 2018b).

Additionally, high iconic words tend to refer to specific entities and are also characterized by higher degrees of abstractness, and emotionality (Calvillo-Torres et al., 2025; de Varda et al., 2025; de Zubicaray & Hinojosa, 2026; Hinojosa et al., 2026; Sidhu, 2027; Winter et al., 2024). Thompson et al. (2020) directly connected these observations to distributional semantics, showing that semantic vectors predict iconicity ratings for English words and American Sign Language signs. Thus, current data indicates that the organization of familiar vocabulary contains information about which meaning patterns are associated with perceived form-meaning resemblance. Furthermore, iconic words tend to be more widely known despite appearing less frequently in everyday speech (Sidhu, 2027). Based on this evidence, here we extend the prediction of iconicity in familiar vocabulary to the interpretation of unfamiliar forms, asking whether information learned from human resemblance judgments predicts the semantic quality and specificity of pseudoword definitions.

Testing this proposal requires distinguishing the production of a possible meaning from its semantic fit, operationalized here in terms of quality and specificity. Semantic quality concerns how closely a definition aligns with the model-derived semantic information associated with its target form, consistent with computational approaches to representing pseudoword semantics and evaluating human-generated definitions (e.g., Chuang et al., 2021; de Varda et al., 2024), while specificity, by contrast, concerns how selectively a definition fits its intended target relative to alternative forms, reflecting the broader distinction between semantic compatibility and informativeness in context (Frank & Goodman, 2012; Degen, 2023). A definition may therefore express a broadly plausible concept while providing relatively little information that distinguishes its intended pseudoword from others, paralleling the distinction between descriptively accurate and discriminative representations (Cohn-Gordon et al., 2018; de Varda et al., 2024). Together, these outcomes distinguish alignment with an interpretation from the relative selectivity of that alignment.

In the present study (see Figure 1 for an overview of the study), we addressed this question by learning mappings from familiar-word representations to human iconicity ratings and applying them to pseudowords, building on approaches that extrapolate lexical judgments from embeddings (Hollis et al., 2017) and transfer learned lexical properties to unfamiliar strings (Gatti & Günther, 2026).

Reanalyzing existing data, we compared letter counts, adjacent bigrams, open bigrams, and fastText embeddings, using 14,750 iconicity-rated English words and 9,560 definitions for 899 pseudowords, and we then computationally indexed pseudoword-definition semantic quality and specificity. If iconicity-related lexical information contributes to novel interpretation, higher predicted iconicity should accompany greater semantic quality and specificity, with the representational comparisons identifying which recoverable information supports this relationship. regression models and predictive performance was evaluated through nested crossvalidation, and models were subsequently refitted on all familiar words and applied to 899 pseudowords without retraining (A). Definition quality was computed as the cosine similarity between each pseudoword and its human-generated definition, whereas definition specificity was calculated by subtracting the mean similarity between that definition and alternative pseudowords from the same collection from its similarity with the target (B). Associations between predicted iconicity and pseudoword-level definition quality and specificity were assessed using collection-adjusted Spearman correlations (C).

Method

Iconicity ratings for existing words

Iconicity ratings were retrieved from the English norms collected by Winter et al. (2024). This dataset contains ratings for 14,776 words, based on 161,057 judgments collected from 1,419 American English speakers. Participants evaluated the perceived resemblance between a word's sound and its meaning on a seven-point scale, ranging from 1 (not iconic at all) to 7 (very iconic). Each word received at least ten valid judgments. These ratings therefore provide an item-level estimate of the extent to which speakers perceive a word's form as resembling its referent or meaning.

For the present analyses, word forms were normalized to lowercase and restricted to alphabetic, single-word entries. The resulting dataset comprised 14,750 distinct words. Mean iconicity ratings served as the dependent variable in the ridge regression analyses described below.

Pseudowords and their definitions

Pseudowords and their definitions were obtained from the two English datasets investigated by de Varda et al. (2024). The first collection contained definitions for 499 pseudowords originally investigated by Gatti, Raveling, et al. (2024) in which the stimuli had been generated using Wuggy (Keuleers & Brysbaert, 2010), with its English orthographic module and constraints on subsyllabic structure, letter length, and transition frequencies. Participants were presented with sets of six pseudowords and selected the items that elicited the most positive and most negative emotional responses; they subsequently provided a plausible definition for each selected item using an affirmative sentence. The second collection contained a different set of 400 pseudowords from the same original set of 1,500 items (i.e., these items were selected from the original stimulus pool after excluding the 499 pseudowords included in the first collection). Participants defined each item using a short affirmative sentence and were instructed to provide a plausible interpretation when the item was unfamiliar.

We applied the published response-quality exclusions to the two collections, removing 74 pseudoword responses. Before embedding extraction, occurrences of the target pseudoword were removed from its definition using case-insensitive whole-token matching. Whitespace was subsequently normalized, and one response that became empty was excluded. This procedure retained 5,609 definitions for the first collection and 3,951 for the second, for a total of 9,560 definitions.

Since the two stimulus sets did not overlap, we pooled their 899 pseudowords and all subsequent association analyses were conducted at the pseudoword level.

(Sub)lexical features

To quantify the information available in orthographic form, we constructed three separate representations: letter counts, adjacent bigram counts, and open bigram counts with identical procedures and feature inventories for existing words and pseudowords.

The letter representation consisted of 26 dimensions corresponding to the letters of the English alphabet, where each dimension encoded the number of occurrences of the corresponding letter in the string. Thus, repeated letters contributed their full counts, and the representation did not encode letter position.

For adjacent bigrams, we first added distinct beginning-and end-of-word markers to each string and then counted every pair of consecutive elements. For example, cat was represented by the pairs #c, ca, at, and t#. The inventory comprised 728 possible features: 676 letter-letter combinations, 26 beginning-marker-letter combinations, and 26 letter-end-marker combinations. Of these, 552 occurred in the existing-word training data.

Open bigrams encoded ordered pairs of elements occurring anywhere within the boundary-marked string. This representation therefore included adjacent pairs as well as nonadjacent pairs, while preserving their relative order. For example, cat additionally contributed the pair ct. Boundary-letter pairs were included, whereas the pair consisting only of the beginning and end markers was excluded.

The inventory again contained 728 possible features, of which 710 occurred in the training data.

Embedding model(s)

FastText

The main embedding model used for the main analyses was fastText (Bojanowski et al., 2017).

Distributional semantic models (DSMs) learn semantic representations from regularities in the linguistic contexts in which words occur, so that words appearing in similar contexts receive similar representations. FastText takes subword information into account by learning vectors for the character n-grams associated with each word, in addition to a vector for the complete lexical item. This solution improves the representation of infrequent words and also allows semantic vectors to be retrieved for strings of letters that are absent from the model's vocabulary. Novel words can therefore be represented by relying on the distributional information associated with their constituent n-grams.

The model used here was trained on English Wikipedia using the skip-gram method, with 300 dimensions, character n-grams of three to six characters, and a context window of five words. As an example, consider the word houses, composed of several three-to six-character n-grams. Its fastText representation is obtained by summing the whole-word vector and the vectors of its constituent ngrams, and then dividing by the number of vectors included in the sum. These include, for example, the trigrams <ho, hou, ous, and es>, the four-grams <hou, hous, and ses>, the five-grams <hous and ouses, and the six-grams <house and houses. Beginning-and end-of-word markers (< and >) are encoded as characters, so that <ho and es>, for example, count as trigrams.

A similar approach can be applied to unattested strings to capture the semantic information associated with novel words. Let's take as an example the string quocky, which is absent from the model's vocabulary. In this case, its representation is obtained by averaging only the vectors of its constituent n-grams, including, for example, the trigrams <qu, quo, uoc, ock, cky, and ky>. Thus, even without a whole-word vector for quocky, the model can extract information learned from its subword units in natural language. Using fastText, we therefore obtained 300-dimensional representations for all words and pseudowords included in the analyses.

Definitions were represented by averaging the native fastText vectors of their constituent content tokens. Specifically, definitions were normalized to Unicode NFC, converted to lowercase, and tokenized into sequences of letters, allowing internal apostrophes. Punctuation separated tokens, and numerical strings were discarded. We removed the 175 English stopwords in the Snowball list (https://snowballstem.org/algorithms/english/stop.txt) and computed the unweighted arithmetic mean of the remaining token vectors. Repeated tokens were retained and contributed repeatedly to this mean. Token vectors were averaged before normalization and then the resulting definition vector was normalized when computing cosine similarity. Three definitions contained no tokens after stopword removal and were excluded from the fastText outcome calculations. The remaining 9,557 definitions provided valid scores for all 899 pseudowords.

The decision to use fastText as the main embedding model was further supported by Chen et al. (2026), who compared five large language models with fastText and human performance in the two experiments performed by Gatti, Rodio, et al. (2024) and showed that fastText more closely reproduced human choices when the response alternatives were pseudowords.

Transformer encoders

To assess whether the results depended on the particular representation used to predict iconicity or evaluate definitions, we additionally considered ten pretrained transformer encoders; these models produce fixed-length embeddings suitable for comparing texts through vector similarity (see Table 1). Their sentence-level training objectives encourage semantically related texts to receive similar representations, extending the sentence-embedding approach described by Reimers and Gurevych (2019).

The model set included BERT-based encoders, a RoBERTa-based sentence encoder, the multilingual XLM-R-based BGE-M3 model, MPNet, and MiniLM. These models differ in their pretrained representations, sentence-embedding training, dimensionality, and aggregation procedures. For example, GIST uses guided selection of contrastive training examples (Solatorio, 2024), whereas supervised SimCSE learns sentence representations using entailment and contradiction relations (Gao et al., 2021). We retained these differences as alternative operationalizations of semantic information. GIST-large (Solatorio, 2024); GTE-large (Li et al., 2023); MiniLM (Wang et al., 2020); Mixedbread Embed Large (Lee et al., 2024); MPNet (Song et al., 2020); SBERT (Reimers & Gurevych, 2019); and SimCSE (Gao et al., 2021). MiniLM and MPNet were used in their sentence-transformers variants linked in the table.

Unlike fastText, these encoders construct representations through bidirectional interactions among the tokens in an input sequence. For a definition, each token's representation is influenced by the surrounding tokens, allowing the final embedding to incorporate contextual and compositional information. The sequence is then reduced to a single vector using the aggregation procedure specified for that model.

Isolated words were submitted as individual input sequences, without a carrier sentence. A word could therefore be represented by one or several subword tokens, together with the model's native special tokens. Pseudowords were processed in exactly the same way. Their representations were constructed from the subword units identified by the tokenizer and the interactions among those units, rather than requiring a vocabulary entry for the complete (pseudo)word. Definitions were submitted as complete cleaned sequences, retaining stopwords, punctuation, and original case before modelspecific tokenization.

Embeddings were retrieved through the Transformers Python library (Wolf et al., 2020) using fixed pretrained checkpoints. Models were evaluated without gradient updates or adaptation to the iconicity ratings or definition data. For mean aggregation, padding positions were excluded using the attention mask, while native special tokens were retained. For CLS aggregation, we extracted the final hidden representation of the initial classification token. For supervised SimCSE, we retained the model's native pooler transformation. E5 inputs received the prefix "query: " for all three input types; the remaining models received no additional prefix.

All encoder embeddings were normalized to unit length and no inputs were truncated. The same checkpoint, tokenizer, prefix, and aggregation procedure were used for existing words, pseudowords, and definitions within each model. The ten encoders used the same set of 9,560 definitions.

Data analysis

Predicting iconicity from (sub)lexical representations

To estimate the iconicity information captured by each representation, we used representational content analysis (RCA; a term proposed by Hussain et al., 2024, but note that the use of embeddings to extrapolate psychologically interpretable judgments predates the RCA label, Hollis et al., 2017).

RCA tests whether a psychologically relevant property is recoverable from the dimensions of a representational space: a mapping is learned between these dimensions and independently measured behavioral judgments, and its predictive performance is evaluated on held-out items. Here, we learned a (ridge) linear mapping from existing-word representations to human iconicity ratings and then applied it to pseudowords represented in the same space, following the approach used by Gatti and Günther (2026) to predict pseudoword memorability. For the semantic models, the resulting predictions therefore index the component of iconicity that is predictable from semantic information.

We first fitted four separate ridge regressions predicting mean human iconicity ratings for the 14,750 existing words from letter counts, adjacent bigram counts, open bigram counts, or the 300 fastText dimensions. Ridge regression applies an L2 penalty to the regression coefficients, allowing correlated and numerous predictors to be included while limiting overfitting. Models were fitted using the glmnet package in R (Friedman et al., 2010), with the mixing parameter set to α = 0, an intercept, and predictor standardization within the training data.

Predictive performance was assessed using nested cross-validation: the words were divided into five outer folds, with each fold serving once as the held-out test set. Within each outer training set, tenfold cross-validation selected the penalty from 100 logarithmically spaced values between 10 4 and 10 -4 . We selected the penalty minimizing cross-validated mean squared error. Performance was calculated from the concatenated outer-fold predictions, ensuring that each word was evaluated using a model trained without that word. We report Spearman correlations between predicted and observed ratings, root mean squared error, and predictive R² , calculated as 𝑅 ! = 1 -""# ""$ , where SSE is the sum of squared prediction errors and SST is the total sum of squared deviations from the observed grand mean.

For prediction of pseudoword iconicity, each model was subsequently fitted to all 14,750 existing words, with the penalty selected through ten-fold cross-validation. The fitted mapping was then applied to the corresponding features of the 899 pseudowords. Overall, these predicted iconicities index the iconicity information recoverable from a given set of features in the representations included.

Definition metrics computation

Firstly, we quantified definition quality as the cosine similarity between the representation of a pseudoword and the representation of a definition provided for that pseudoword. Cosine similarity is the most widely used measure of semantic similarity in distributional semantic models (Günther et al., 2019; Turney & Pantel, 2010). It is the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their Euclidean norms, and therefore compares their directions independently of their magnitudes:

Here, 𝐩 % denotes the vector for pseudoword 𝑖, and 𝐝 %& denotes the vector for its 𝑗th definition. Higher values indicate stronger alignment between the semantic information associated with the pseudoword and the content expressed in the definition; this measure therefore operationalizes definition quality as semantic correspondence. We calculated the score separately for each definition and then averaged these scores within pseudoword.

Then, we assessed whether a definition was particularly aligned with its intended pseudoword relative to other pseudowords. For each definition, specificity was calculated by subtracting its mean cosine similarity with all other pseudowords from the same original collection from its similarity with the intended target:

Here, 𝐶 ' denotes the set of pseudowords in collection 𝑠, and 𝑁 ' is the number of pseudowords in that collection. The comparison therefore involved 498 alternative pseudowords for the first collection and 399 for the second.

Higher specificity indicates that a definition is more closely associated with its intended pseudoword than with the alternatives available in that collection; this measure thus indexes target discrimination.

As for quality, specificity was calculated separately for each definition and subsequently averaged within pseudoword.

Associations between predicted iconicity and definition scores

Then we performed the main analyses, which related the four predicted iconicity scores to fastTextbased definition quality and specificity. Because the two collections differed in their designs, associations were adjusted for collection membership. Predictor and outcome scores were first converted to ranks across all 899 pseudowords, using average ranks for ties. We then removed collection-specific means from the ranks and correlated the resulting residuals. The resulting coefficients are collection-adjusted Spearman correlations.

Two-sided significance tests used 4,999 permutations of pseudoword predictor scores within collection. The same permutations were used across representations, and p-values were calculated with a +1 correction, yielding a minimum attainable p value of .0002. Unadjusted 95% confidence intervals were obtained from 2,000 bootstrap samples of pseudowords, stratified by collection, with ranks recomputed in each sample.

The four predictors and two metrics yielded eight main tests, to which we applied the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) to control the false discovery rate. We report the resulting adjusted p values, labeled as q, alongside raw p values.

Robustness analyses across semantic representations

Finally, to evaluate whether the association depended on using fastText both to predict iconicity and to score definitions, we repeated the iconicity-training procedure separately for each of the ten transformer encoders. Each ridge model used only that encoder's vector dimensions and was trained on the same 14,750 words, using the same outer folds, inner folds, penalty grid, and selection criterion as the main models. We then predicted iconicity for the same 899 pseudowords.

First, the ten encoder-based iconicity predictions were correlated with the fastText quality and specificity scores. These 20 tests changed the representation used to predict iconicity while holding the definition metric constant.

Second, we crossed all eleven vector-based iconicity predictors (i.e., fastText and the ten encoders) with quality and specificity scores computed using each of the eleven representations.
