This produced two directional 11 × 11 matrices, one for each outcome. All robustness analyses used the same collection-adjusted correlations, permutation procedure, and bootstrap procedure as the main analyses. These robustness tests are reported with raw p values.

Results

All four feature sets predicted iconicity ratings in held-out words (Figure 2). The letter model achieved a predictive R² of .135, with a Spearman correlation of .353 between predicted and observed ratings and an RMSE of .832. Adjacent bigrams achieved R² = .210, ρ = .423, and RMSE = .795, whereas open bigrams achieved R² = .171, ρ = .385, and RMSE = .815.

The fastText model had the highest predictive performance among the four main models, with R² = .315, ρ = .515, and RMSE = .741. Thus, a linear mapping from the fastText dimensions accounted for approximately 31.5% of the variance in iconicity ratings under held-out evaluation. Representational content analysis of iconicity ratings for 14,750 English words using letters, adjacent bigrams, open bigrams, and fastText dimensions.

We next examined whether the iconicity predictions generalized to differences in the definitions provided for pseudowords (Figure 3). FastText-based predicted iconicity was positively associated with definition quality, ρ = .175, 95% CI [.111, .234], p = .0002, q = .0008. Pseudowords receiving higher predicted iconicity scores therefore elicited definitions that were more closely aligned with their fastText representations. A comparable association was observed for definition specificity, ρ = .174, 95% CI [.108, .236], p = .0002, q = .0008, where higher predicted iconicity was associated with definitions that distinguished their intended pseudoword more strongly from other pseudowords in the same collection. The three orthographic predictors showed associations close to zero for both outcomes. None was significant after correction, with all six q values equal to .9970.

These results indicate that the component of iconicity recovered from fastText representations was associated with both the semantic alignment and target specificity of pseudoword definitions 1.

Although orthographic features predicted iconicity ratings for existing words, their resulting pseudoword predictions showed no association with either definition measure.

Robustness analyses

Each encoder supported prediction of existing-word iconicity under nested cross-validation (Figure 4A). Predictive R² ranged from .315 for MiniLM-L12 to .391 for E5-large-v2. E5-large-v2 had the highest numerical performance, followed by SimCSE BERT-large (R² = .382) and SBERT RoBERTa-large (R² = .375).

The encoder models were then applied to the pseudowords, and their iconicity predictions were related to the fastText definition scores (Figure 4B and Figure 4C). All ten predictors showed positive associations with both outcomes. Nine of the ten quality associations were significant at the p < .05 level, with MiniLM-L12 as the exception, and eight of the ten specificity associations were significant, with MiniLM-L12 and MPNet as the exceptions. Among the encoder predictors, SimCSE BERT-large showed the largest numerical associations with fastText quality, ρ = .164, 95% CI [.102, .224], p = .0002, and specificity, ρ = .143, 95% CI [.079, .204], p = .0002.

1 As an additional control, to assess whether the observed effects could be explained by (trivial) orthographic similarity to familiar word forms, we recomputed definition quality and specificity after replacing each pseudoword's fastText vector with the vector of its closest orthographic neighbor among the model's 20,000 most frequent words. Spearman correlations between fastText-predicted iconicity and these new measures were negligible for both definition quality (ρ = .008, p = .804) and specificity (ρ = -.005, p = .886) and were significantly smaller than those obtained using the pseudoword vectors (p < .001). Thus, these results argue against the explanation that the original associations simply reflect the trivial activation of the closest orthographically similar familiar words. The positive associations therefore generalized to iconicity predictions derived from several representations other than fastText. Their magnitudes varied across encoders, and stronger prediction of existing-word iconicity did not necessarily correspond to a stronger association with pseudoword definition scores. For example, E5-large-v2 achieved the highest word-prediction R² , whereas SimCSE BERT-large showed the strongest associations with the fastText outcomes among the ten encoders.

We next examined all combinations of the eleven iconicity predictors and eleven definition metrics (Figure 4B and Figure 4C). For definition quality, 120 of the 121 correlations were positive, and 102 had p < .05. For specificity, 118 of the 121 correlations were positive, and 92 were significant. To focus on associations that could not arise solely from using exactly the same representation in both stages, we examined the off-diagonal cells separately. All 110 off-diagonal quality correlations were positive, and 92 were significant with p < .05. For specificity, 108 of the 110 off-diagonal correlations were positive, and 82 were significant. Off-diagonal correlations ranged from .005 to .320 for quality and from -.010 to .317 for specificity.

The association between semantically predictable iconicity and definition scores therefore extended across different representations used for iconicity prediction and definition evaluation. This pattern indicates that the results were not confined to the reuse of fastText in both stages. At the same time, the variation in effect sizes shows that the strength of the association depended on how semantic information was represented and measured.

Discussion

In the present study, we investigated whether iconicity-related information learned from familiar vocabulary is associated with the meanings people construct for unfamiliar forms. Across 899 pseudowords, higher fastText-derived iconicity predictions accompanied definitions with greater semantic quality and specificity. Notably, by transferring a mapping learned from familiar-word resemblance judgments to unfamiliar forms, these findings connect the semantic organization of perceived iconicity with variation in novel meaning construction.

Theoretically, this pattern favors a continuous account of lexical knowledge in which learned formmeaning relations remain productive beyond the particular items through which they were acquired.

Discriminative theories formalize this possibility as mappings between sublexical cues and distributed semantic information (Baayen et al., 2019), with such mappings also predicting aspects of pseudoword comprehension and production (Chuang et al., 2021). Within this perspective, a novel form elicits a semantic response through previously learned relations. Our findings complement this framework by identifying iconicity-related structure as a dimension along which familiar-word knowledge generalizes to explicit interpretation, extending evidence from semantic priming, affective judgments, and meaning selection (Gatti et al., 2023; Gatti, Raveling, et al., 2024; Gatti, Rodio, et al., 2024). Notably, this extension connects two processes that are often considered separately: the perception of motivated relationships between form and meaning, and the use of accumulated lexical knowledge to interpret a form that has no established meaning. Crucially, the fact that fastTextderived iconicity predictions, but not predictions based on letter or bigram information alone, were associated with the semantic properties of pseudoword definitions suggests that the information relevant to novel meaning construction cannot be reduced to formal resemblance. Rather, it may depend on the relationships between sublexical patterns and the meanings with which they have become associated throughout linguistic experience. In this sense, iconicity-related information may provide a particularly informative dimension through which previously acquired lexical knowledge generalizes to unfamiliar forms. The present results suggest that these processes may be related insofar as the regularities associated with iconicity in familiar words provide information relevant to constructing meanings for pseudowords. This account does not require unfamiliar forms to possess an intrinsically "correct" meaning, but instead, their interpretation may reflect the extent to which their properties are compatible with semantic patterns established through linguistic experience cosnistesnt with prior research showing that several sematic factors contribute to iconicity (such as the tendency to depict specific references, or to show higher degrees of abstractness, emotionality or sensory referents; Calvillo-Torres et al., 2025; de Varda et al., 2025; Sidhu, 2027; Winter et al., 2024).

The specificity result gives this account particular theoretical weight because it concerns the selectivity of a form-meaning relationship. Higher embedding-derived iconicity predictions accompanied definitions that aligned more strongly with their intended pseudoword relative to competing forms. This pattern motivates an account of interpretation as graded activation among semantic possibilities, consistent with models in which distributed meaning representations compete during word recognition (Rodd et al., 2004). That is, prior linguistic experience supplies different degrees of support for candidate interpretations, making some meanings more compatible with a particular form than others. The semantic structure associated with iconicity can therefore be conceived as a source of probabilistic constraints on meaning construction, organizing candidate interpretations while allowing individual knowledge and context to influence the interpretation ultimately expressed. Importantly, the association with specificity suggests that iconicity-related information may do more than facilitate the generation of broadly plausible meanings: it may also contribute to distinguishing among alternative interpretations, increasing the extent to which a definition captures the semantic properties associated with a particular novel form.

This proposal also connects the semantic patterning of iconicity with the complementary functions of resemblance and arbitrariness in language. Iconicity varies systematically across semantic regions, including sensory meanings (Thompson et al., 2020; Winter et al., 2017), whereas arbitrary forms can support abstraction beyond specific sensory depictions (Lupyan & Winter, 2018). Within this broader division, iconicity-related regularities offer resources for selecting and differentiating interpretations, alongside the categorical flexibility supported by conventional lexical knowledge.

Our results locate this relationship at the productive interface between familiar vocabulary and unfamiliar forms, connecting the organization of iconic meanings with the construction of new semantic associations (Dingemanse et al., 2015; Winter et al., 2024).

Our findings also contribute to theories of iconicity by demonstrating that iconic resemblance and distributional generalization are complementary cognitive mechanisms, rather than competing ones.

Rather than viewing iconicity as a direct replication of external reality, our data can be interpreted in light of proposals like the analogue-building model (Emmorey, 2014). This account suggests that linguistic iconicity relies on structured cognitive mapping between schematic representations of multimodal experiences (i.e., perceptual, motor and affective), and semantic representations (Emmorey, 2014; Hinojosa et al., 2027). Our data extend this view by highlighting the role of statistical linguistic experience. Specifically, we propose that familiar lexical patterns act as scaffolds that organize and facilitate access to resemblance-related semantic information when individuals interpret novel or unfamiliar labels (Perniss et al., 2010; Sidhu & Pexman, 2018a). Consequently, interpreting a novel form may involve more than detecting a resemblance between its physical properties and a potential referent, as it may also involve drawing on previously acquired regularities that link similar forms to related semantic representations.

Consistent with this idea, we suggest that the relationship between form and meaning may be shaped both by the perceptual and experiential correspondences that make certain forms seem motivated and by the distributional structure through which those correspondences become established and available for generalization. These components need not be mutually exclusive: experiential correspondences may contribute to the emergence of motivated form-meaning relationships, while linguistic experience organizes and reinforces the regularities through which such relationships can be extended to new forms. By bridging the gap between experiential grounding and learned form-meaning relations, our perspective broadly aligns with theories that link embodied resemblance with the statistical organization of lexical knowledge (Andrews et al., 2014; Louwerse, 2018) and, more specifically, with hybrid accounts of conceptual combination that deal with the processes involved in generating new meaning from old referents (Feldman & Narayanan, 2004; Lynott & Connell, 2010).

The embodied conceptual combination model, for instance, assumes that the representation of new concepts is built upon the interaction between multimodal simulations based on perceptual, motor, affective, introspective, or social experiences and linguistic distributional information (Lynott & Connell, 2010). In particular, the crossed-model analyses establish that this association recurs across different representational approaches and architectures, indicating that it can be recovered through several operationalizations of semantic information. Performance depended on both the task and each representation's role, potentially reflecting differences in how models training organizes semantic similarity. Training on diverse text pairs, as implemented in E5 and GTE, can support broad semantic coverage, while the selection of informative contrasts can sharpen distinctions between related and unrelated interpretations (Li et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2022). GIST explicitly guides the selection of negative examples, whereas supervised SimCSE uses entailment and contradiction pairs, providing different routes to organizing such distinctions (Gao et al., 2021; Solatorio, 2024). MiniLM's compressed architecture may partly explain its weaker performance, although the variation among larger encoders also points to the importance of training objectives and the resulting similarity structure (Wang et al., 2020). Specifically, predicting iconicity from familiar-word vectors requires relevant information to be recoverable, whereas the pseudoword analyses additionally depend on how unfamiliar forms and definitions are positioned relative to one another. Generalization to unfamiliar forms therefore provides a complementary criterion for evaluating which aspects of lexical knowledge different representations preserve.

Two further theoretical implications can follow from these findings. First, the present results suggest a connection between learned lexical regularities and the processes through which lexical invention becomes interpretable in communication. Accounts of lexical innovation emphasize shared knowledge and the circumstances in which an expression is used (Clark & Clark, 1979), while probabilistic accounts of pragmatic inference explain interpretation through the integration of linguistic information, contextual expectations, and assumptions about informativeness (Frank & Goodman, 2012). Our findings suggest that iconicity-related patterns in familiar vocabulary may contribute to this process by making some interpretations of an unfamiliar form more plausible than others. These graded semantic expectations could provide a starting point for contextual and communicative inference, helping listeners identify what a speaker intends to convey. This perspective connects spontaneous meaning construction with purposeful lexical invention: in both cases, accumulated lexical knowledge may constrain the interpretations available for a form without an established meaning. It predicts that compatibility with familiar lexical patterns and communicative context jointly influence the meaning assigned to a novel expression.

Second, the findings connect this account of meaning construction with the proposed role of iconicity in language acquisition. Iconicity is widespread across spoken and signed vocabularies (Perlman et al., 2018; Perniss et al., 2010), with evidence linking it to semantic aspects of language learning and adult lexical processing (Ortega, 2017; Vinson et al., 2015). The sound-symbolism bootstrapping hypothesis proposes that correspondences between linguistic forms and conceptual properties can help learners identify potential referents and establish form-meaning associations (Imai & Kita, 2014; see also Sidhu, 2026) and developmental evidence indicates that sensitivity to these correspondences changes with age and experience (Fort et al., 2018), while their contribution to learning depends on the particular associations and tasks involved (Nielsen & Dingemanse, 2021). Adults can also use sound-symbolic information to interpret words from unfamiliar languages (Revill et al., 2014; Van Hoey et al., 2023). The present study extends this perspective to the spontaneous construction of meanings for (written) pseudowords. The pattern observed here, consistent with the idea that adults drawing on learned semantic regularities associated with iconicity to constrain novel meanings, therefore suggests that iconicity-related lexical knowledge remains productive in adulthood and motivates the prediction that these initial interpretive constraints may also facilitate subsequent word learning.

In conclusion, iconicity-related information recovered from familiar-word representations predicts both the semantic alignment and target specificity of human-generated pseudoword definitions. These findings support a productive view of lexical knowledge, with established vocabulary supplying graded constraints on the construction of unfamiliar meanings. By connecting human resemblance judgments with the alignment and selectivity of novel definitions, the present study identifies iconicity-related semantic structure as a predictor of novel meaning construction, showing how patterns associated with resemblance in established vocabulary extend to the interpretation of new forms.

The study re-analyzed public data comprising iconicity ratings from Winter et al. (2024) available at https://osf.io/qvw6u/ and pseudoword definitions from de Varda et al. (2024) available at https://osf.io/5bv8r/.

The representational comparison clarifies which iconicity-related information accompanies this variation. Letter counts and both bigram representations predicted iconicity ratings for held-out existing words, yet their pseudoword predictions showed associations close to zero with definition scores. FastText-derived predictions, conversely, related to both outcomes supporting an account in which unfamiliar forms acquire interpretive potential through their connections to accumulated (sub)lexical and semantic knowledge. This contrast is particularly informative because it suggests that the information supporting iconicity judgments for familiar words is not necessarily sufficient to explain how people construct meanings for unfamiliar forms. Although surface-level orthographic properties may capture some of the formal regularities associated with perceived iconicity, they do not appear to provide the information required to account for the semantic properties of novel definitions. In the present analyses, associations with definition scores emerged only when formrelated information was represented within a space that also captured distributional relationships across the lexicon. It should also be noted that form remains (partially) central because fastText constructs pseudoword representations from character n-grams whose vectors are learned through their occurrence in the lexicon (Bojanowski et al., 2017). Thus, fastText does not simply discard formal information in favor of meaning; rather, it captures how sublexical patterns are embedded in the lexical environments in which they occur. The relevant information therefore concerns how sublexical information distribution connect to learned meanings, beyond letter or bigram counts alone.

The control analysis further clarifies this distinction. Replacing each pseudoword vector with the vector of its closest orthographic neighbor among the model's 20,000 most frequent words yielded negligible associations with definition quality and specificity and these associations were significantly smaller than those obtained with the original pseudoword representations. The observed relationship therefore cannot readily be explained by the contribution of a single familiar word selected on the basis of orthographic similarity. Instead, it is consistent with the possibility that the relevant information reflects broader distributional regularities across the lexicon. A novel form may share sublexical properties with familiar words without simply inheriting the meaning of its closest orthographic neighbor. This distinction suggests that the interpretive potential of an unfamiliar form may depend on how its features relate to patterns distributed across multiple lexical items. Although the present analyses do not establish the precise mechanism through which these relationships influence human interpretation, they indicate that orthographic resemblance to a single known word is insufficient to account for the observed associations.
